Data-Driven Proﬁle Prediction

Data-Driven Proﬁle Prediction for DIII-D J. Abbate a,1, 2 R. Conlin a,3, 2 and E. Kolemen3, 2

1)Dept. of Astrophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA 2)Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ 08543, USA 3)Dept. of Mechanical Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

(Dated: 30 September 2020)

A new, fully data-driven algorithm has been developed that uses neural networks to predict plasma proﬁles on a scale of τE into the future given actuators and the present plasma state. The model was trained and tested on DIII-D data from the 2013-2018 experimental campaigns. The model is accurate on average, with q predictions the worst and pressure predictions the best. The model can run in milliseconds and is very simple to use. This makes it a potentially useful tool for operators and physicists when planning plasma scenarios. It also is a candidate for doing phase-space exploration without going through the DIII- D database or complicated and computationally expensive simulation codes. A reduced model using only realtime diagnostics has also been developed and formed the basis for a model-predictive control algorithm implemented and successfully tested on DIII-D.

Keywords: DIII-D, machine learning, neural networks, transport

## I. INTRODUCTION

Validated whole-device tokamak modeling is a primary focus of modern fusion energy research. Given device parameters and the trajectory of actuators over time, we would like to simulate the evolution of important properties of the plasma. A variety of possible machines and plasma scenarios can then be inferred without spending billions of dollars on a new device or millions on a series of experiments. A host of workﬂows exist for so-called “ﬂight simulation” of plasma proﬁle evolution. Full-f methods like XGC [1] and GKEYLL [2] evolve the full plasma pro- ﬁle forward on short turbulence timescales. They are very computationally expensive but include most of the physics, though even this approach may have limitations for describing real experiments [3]. For less timeintensive approximations, a variety of integrated modeling frameworks have been built to iteratively calculate ﬂux coeﬃcients on turbulent timescales then use the coef- ﬁcients to integrate diﬀusion-like equations on transport timescales [4]. Popular codes for facilitating this work- ﬂow include TRANSP [5], JINTRAC [6], CRONOS [7], JETTO [8], and (steady-state only) TGYRO [9] or TRINITY [10]. Transport coeﬃcients can be determined by gyrokinetic plasma microturbulence codes, such as GYRO [11] and GENE [12]; and CGYRO [13]. These δf codes, though computationally cheaper than full-f, still generally require months of CPU hours to get transport coeﬃcients. However, the quasilinear approximation [14, 15] can be used to reduce this time down to seconds while maintaining reasonable results, at least in

the core. These estimates are believed to be quite close to both the nonlinear calculations and experiment (see e.g. TGLF validated with GYRO [16]), though there are still regimes with discrepancies [10]. Modern codes implementing this technique include QuaLiKiz [17], TGLF [18], MMM95 [19], and GLF23 [20]. For Hmode operation, a prediction for the pedestal height and width, whether a guess or from a pedestal model like EPED [21], is required as a boundary condition when edge predictions are unavailable or inaccurate. Additionally, all types of models require separate codes for calculating deposition from particle and heat sources (e.g. NUBEAM [22] for neutral beams and GENRAY [23] for ECH). Another downside to the workﬂow is that, even with the quasilinear approximation, each step (other than equilibrium ﬁtting) takes order of minutes to run. This not only disqualiﬁes the workﬂow from realtime control, but also slows down scientists looking for back-of-theenvelope estimates. For this reason, neural networks have been trained on broad databases of previous simulations to interpolate between them. For example, researchers have already applied this mechanism to approximate TGLF [24], QuaLiKiz [25], EPED [24], and NUBEAM [26]. A neural net for approximating transport coeﬃcients has also been trained on experimental (calculated via autoONETWO) DIII-D data [27]. This paper demonstrates the performance of a ﬁrstof-its-kind neural network that predicts plasma proﬁles 200ms into the future on DIII-D given information on the present proﬁles, present 0D plasma parameters, and future information on the actuator settings. Rather than requiring a sequence of models and approximations with their compounding inaccuracies, this is a simple inputoutput mapping between what physicists control (the actuators) and the metric that physicists care about (the

In section II we outline the model architecture and training procedure. In section III we demonstrate performance over a database of never-before-seen shots.

## II. MACHINE LEARNING MODEL

The time evolution of the plasma state can be generically described by a diﬀerential equation of the form:

dx

dt = f(x, u) (1)

where x is a vector of the plasma state, consisting of the values of the proﬁles suitably discretized in space, and u is a vector of control inputs. This can be put in a discrete time form:

xt+1 = xt + f(xt, ut) (2)

where t is a time index. In this paper, we attempt to approximate the function f using a neural network. Machine learning has already proven itself to perform as good or better than the state-of-the-art for a variety of fusion tasks. Event prediction, such as for disruptions and instabilities, is a particularly well-explored area. Various shallow learning algorithms have been applied, such as support vector machines [28], discriminant analysis [29], classiﬁcation and regression trees [30], and random forests [31, 32]. Neural networks also have a long history in event prediction, employed by researchers at TEXT [33], DIII-D [34], ASDEX [35], JET [36], JT- 60U [37], and ADITYA [38]. More recently, a disruption predictor combining recurrent and convolutional neural networks was developed, which helped inspire the architecture for the present work [39]. Most of these algorithms were tested on tokamaks in realtime, demonstrating that machine learning not only can provide state-ofthe-art accuracy but also can be useful for control.

## A. Data Processing

Data is loaded and partially processed within the OM- FIT framework [40]. A new module has been developed for this task and is publicly available within OMFIT a. The processing, along with the model training, is done on 1 NVIDIA V100 GPU and 8 IBM POWER9 CPU cores on Princeton University’s Traverse computing cluster. This code is also publicly available, on GitHub b.

a “SIGNAL PROCESSING” module in the “pro- ﬁle prediction data processing” branch b https://github.com/jabbate7/plasma-proﬁle-predictor

DIII-D shots from 2013 through the 2018 campaign are collected from the MDS+ database [41]. Shots with a pulse length less than 2s, a normalized plasma beta less than 1, or a non-standard tokamak divertor topology are excluded from the start. A variety of non-standard data is also excluded, including the following situations:

1. during and after a dudtrip trigger

2. during and after ECH activation, since ECH is not currently included as an actuator

3. whenever density feedback is oﬀ

4. during and after non-normal operation of internal coils

All signals are then put on the same 50ms time base by averaging all signal values available between the present time and 50ms prior. If no data is available in the window, the most recent value is ﬂoated. Only time steps during current ﬂattop, and where all signals are available, are included. The model considers data in 50ms non-overlapping chunks, a spacing large enough to smooth over most variations in modulated signals like the injected power. Each chunk corresponds to a single “timestep”. There are three fundamental types of data we consider: plasma proﬁles, plasma parameters, and actuators. The plasma state is determined by the plasma proﬁles and the parameters. Proﬁles are 1-dimensional signals like temperature and density. Parameters are 0-dimensional signals like average density and shape parameters. Actuators are knobs that are set by the operator, including injected power and target current. A full list of signals used by the algorithm is shown in Table I. The model takes in actuator and plasma parameter signals 6 timesteps (i.e. 300ms) into the past. It takes in the proﬁles at the present timestep. And it takes in a “proposal” for the actuators at each of 4 timesteps (200ms) into the future. Throughout the paper, we will call this full set of information a “sample”. With the sample as input, the algorithm predicts the change in each of the proﬁles 200ms (4 timesteps) into the future. This 200ms prediction window was chosen based on the typical energy conﬁnement time (τE) at DIII-D, and was empirically found to be a period over which the proﬁles change noticeably while not so long that the future state cannot be reliably predicted. The lookback of 300ms (6 timesteps) was determined by trial and error, and also by rough estimates of correlation times between actuator inputs and proﬁle response. Temperature, density and rotation proﬁles are from Zipﬁt c, while pressure and rotational transform are from EFIT [42]. Zipﬁt proﬁles are linearly interpolated onto

## B. Model Architecture

A sketch of the model architecture is shown in Figure 1. Given the spatially distributed information contained in the plasma proﬁles, we take inspiration from image classiﬁcation models and use a sequence of convolutional layers to attempt to capture local eﬀects in the proﬁles, such as gradients and transport coeﬃcients. Using multiple convolutional layers with varying kernel sizes has been shown to help the model learn information over a wide range of spatial scales [43] [44]. Multiple pro- ﬁles are also processed at the same time, with each proﬁle treated as a “channel” of a 1D image (cf, RGB channels for a 2D image). This allows the model to learn correlations between the diﬀerent proﬁles. Each layer expands the number of channels and the ﬁnal output of the initial convolutional layers is an array of size n × m, where n

is the number of spatial points (33) and m is a hyperparameter to be tuned (denoted as “Channels”, discussed further in section II D). Each channel of this array can be considered a “feature proﬁle” that is a nonlinear combination of the various input proﬁles.

The activation function used in all layers is ReLU, which we empirically found to perform the best. The general idea of the architecture - to start with smaller kernels and expand to larger ones then do the reverse - has been demonstrated to capture many spatial scales of information in the popular edge-detection algorithm UNet.

The parameter and actuator data is fed through a series of fully connected and Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) layers [45]. The fully connected layers attempt to measure the eﬀect of the given actuator or parameter at each spatial point in the plasma, while the LSTM layers look over the time history of the signals to account

for the fact that in many cases it takes time for a given actuator to propagate its eﬀect through the plasma. The ﬁnal output from this section of the model is again an array of size n × m, which is then added to the “feature proﬁles” output by the initial convolutional layers. This combination of proﬁle and actuator information is then fed through a second sequence of convolutional layers, with a unique output path for each predicted pro- ﬁle. Each of these output paths reduce the m “feature proﬁles” down to a single output proﬁle, which is the models estimate of the given proﬁle 200ms in the future. All layers in the network use the ReLU activation function, which has good performance and ease of training [46][47]. The one exception is the LSTM layers, which use a hard sigmoid function for their recurrent activation. This bounds the output, which helps to improve convergence during training [48].

## C. Model Training

The goal of a neural network is to approximate a function by optimizing the parameters of a model (described above). The neural network can be described by a function of the form

f(x, u, θ) (3)

where x and u are the state and control, and θ are the weights to be learned through training. Training consists of attempting to ﬁnd the weights θ∗that minimize a cost function. In our case, the cost function is a mean squared error. The optimization problem can then be expressed as

θ∗= argmin θ

where i is an index that ranges over all N samples in the training dataset. We use Keras [49] with a backend of Tensorﬂow to manage the traditional neural net training workﬂow. Over the training set, the package computes the steepestdescent step in the loss function over the model-weight space and saves it. After trial-and-error, we chose a batch size of 128. So after every 128th randomly selected sample, the package does a pseudo-average (we use the adaptive gradient optimization algorithm [50]) of the previous 128 samples and then updates the model weights and recomputes the derivatives to be used for computing the steepest-descent paths for the next batch of 128 samples. We repeat this process over the entire dataset for 200 epochs. This entire process takes about 5 hours. We ﬁrst split our data so that 10% of shots are reserved for testing, and the other 90% of shots are sliced into samples. We use a random 20% of those samples for validation during hyperparameter tuning, and the rest for training. All plots in section III are from data in the test set, which includes 13,196 samples from a separate 340 randomly selected shots.

## D. Model Tuning

Another key choice in machine learning models are the hyperparameters, such as layer type, hidden layer sizes, type of activation function, and diﬀerent data normalization and weighting schemes. We follow the classic machine learning workﬂow. For a variety of possible models (deﬁned by their hyperparameter values), the training set is used to stochastically optimize the model weights. We then compute the loss function for each of the models over the validation set and choose the model which yields the best performance. Initial random-hyperparameter searches demonstrated clear dominance of some hyperparameters over others. For example, we considered both convolutional and fully connected layers. It was found that the convolutional layers systematically performed signiﬁcantly better than fully connected, which can be physically understood by recalling that convolutional layers have a ﬁxed spatial extent, and only couple local information, which matches with the local gradients that drive transport equations. We also considered models which take in and predict the ﬁrst few Principal Component Analysis modes (see section III) of proﬁles rather than the realspace representation, and the real-space representation systematically performed better. Finally, we tried a variety of custom loss functions for training which weighted the edge of the proﬁle more than the core, since that is where the important pedestal behavior lies. Although this indeed gave better performance at the edge, for simplicity we decided to continue using losses that weight all real-space points equally. We then used a ﬁxed-grid hyperparameter tuning process to arrive at the ﬁnal hyperparameter values. It was found that supplying the model with parameters to describe the plasma shape improved performance. We believe this was due to the shape parameters allowing the model to infer information about compression of the plasma which can lead to density and temperature increases. Another consideration was what combination of input proﬁles would give the best predictions, and which target proﬁles are predictable using a given set of inputs. To do this we trained models with and without the use of pressure and rotational transform proﬁles from EFIT, and examined diﬀerent versions of EFIT data. Speciﬁ- cally, EFIT01 is a magnetics only reconstruction of the equilibrium, and so is generally only accurate for estimating global parameters. EFIT02 uses motional Stark eﬀect data to constrain the safety factor proﬁle and so is generally a more accurate estimate of the equilibrium. Models were trained to predict temperature, density, and plasma rotation, using those proﬁles as inputs. Then additional models were trained that also included pressure and rotational transform data from EFIT01 and EFIT02. As shown in Figure 2, including this additional data resulted in better predictions for temperature, density, and plasma rotation. However, despite proﬁles from

This could be due to EFIT01 data being available for more shots, leading to a slightly larger training set, or could be due to the higher ﬁdelity EFIT02 data containing more detail than is strictly necessary, making the relevant information harder to extract. Work is currently underway to build a large training database of kinetically constrained equilibria using CAKE [51] which will be used to train future models. The ﬁnal hyperparameter we considered was weighting samples diﬀerently during training. It was observed that many of the shots in the training set are fairly similar, and across many timesteps the proﬁles can be roughly constant. One common method to mitigate the eﬀects of an unbalanced training set is by weighting the samples relative to their frequency. This is easiest to implement for classiﬁcation tasks with a ﬁnite number of classes, where the number of members of each class can serve as the weighting parameter. This can be diﬃcult for regression problems, where the number of classes is effectively inﬁnite, so we opted for a simpler approach of weighting the samples by the total variation of the actuators in the 300ms lookback window. This imbalance and similarity in the training data will be discussed further in section IV. We found that weighting the samples in this fashion did improve performance on average and led to the best performing models when combined with the other choices of hyperparameters. We suggest that this weighting eﬀectively instructed the model to focus more

on samples with large variations, which would help it to learn the dominant physics driving transport.

## III. MODEL PERFORMANCE

Perhaps the most straightforward way to evaluate the accuracy of the machine learning model is to plot the model predictions vs experimental measurements and see how well they match visually. This is done for a representative sample in Figure 3. The model is given as input the true proﬁles at time t, shown in orange, along with information about actuators and the shape of the plasma. It predicts the proﬁles 200ms later, shown in blue, which agree quite well with the true values at t+200ms, shown in dotted black. Note that the predictions were not constrained to be smooth, though this could be done as a post-processing step depending on the application. While proﬁles should not be smoothed for control applications or getting global parameters like the average or PCA components, one may want to smooth if being used for human analysis or as input to other codes. To get a better idea of how the machine learning model performs on the overall dataset, one possibility is to look at the error in the machine learning model’s predictions vs a baseline prediction, averaged over the whole test dataset. The baseline model selected for comparison is one that predicts no change in the proﬁle. We note that there is not a strong physical motivation for such an assumption, but it was found empirically to be a better approximation than any other simple approximation the authors tried (including linear regression). For many shots, the proﬁles do not change much, so this baseline is statistically a rather good estimate of the true behavior. In Figure 4 we plot the absolute error vs spatial coordinate for each proﬁle for both the model and baseline, averaged over all samples in the test set. In all cases, the machine learning model performs as good or better than the baseline. Given that the model predicts entire 1-dimensional proﬁles, it is useful to have a meaningful scalar quantity that can be used to determine how well the model performs. One useful metric is the accuracy of the model in capturing the Principle Component Analysis (PCA) modes of the proﬁles. PCA works by ﬁnding an orthogonal set of basis vectors for a given dataset, with the desirable feature that the ﬁrst PCA mode captures the maximum possible variance in the dataset, while the second mode captures the most possible variance while being orthogonal to the ﬁrst mode, and in general the ith mode captures the maximum possible variance while remaining orthogonal to all modes j < i. Using the PCA modes as basis functions, we can decompose a given proﬁle as

## IV. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION

We demonstrated that a machine learning model can successfully capture the correct scaling with actuators and proﬁle relaxations on average. The model can run in milliseconds and is very simple to use. In particular, unlike predictive transport solvers that sometimes don’t converge and require a lot of tuning and expert knowledge, this is a simple input-output model. This makes it a potentially useful tool for operators and physicists when planning plasma scenarios. It also is a candidate for doing phase-space exploration without searching the DIII- D database or executing expensive simulation codes. Finally, we have already successfully implemented a modelpredictive control algorithm into DIII-D using a reduced version of the model that runs in hundreds of microseconds and reads only realtime information. A paper on this work is forthcoming. Shots tend to be reloaded from previous experiments when testing new physics, so that despite having thousands of shots many are very similar. In general neural nets ﬁnd the easiest way to match its target, and so could be learning to identify the relatively small number of discharge patterns rather then recognizing physics of transport and source deposition. Whether the neural net is learning useful patterns or simply memorizing past discharge evolution is diﬃcult to answer. One imperfect methodology for future work would be to compare the neural net’s predicted response to each actuator with that of a theoretical model. This would allow independent and ﬂexible variation of the inputs. Another mechanism will be our planned experiments allowing the model to control the plasma in real-time through a variety of unseen scenarios. Finally, having a larger database of shots where semi-random changes to actuators are made during ﬂattop would be a helpful supplement to the existing DIII-D database. In addition to helping improve datadriven models, this would also help develop and validate physics-based models. In addition to exploring how the model works, there

are also a few techniques to make the model perform even better. First, some information is still missing. For example, ﬂuctuation (from ECE or BES) and radial electric ﬁeld measurements may help. More challenging would be including wall-condition information (such as how recently the machine was boronized). Second, it would be nice in the future to predict more proﬁles (such as ion temperature) and use more actuators (such as shape control and ECH). Finally, a relative disadvantage of machine learning models is lack of robustness and inability to extrapolate beyond the data. Combining these predictions with physics-based models would be the best way to increase model robustness while more easily allowing extrapolation to future devices. This would also allow us to better understand why the model predicts the way it does.
